newsitem.title: GERMANY: Expatriates track US poll at all-night parties.
newsitem.headline: Expatriates track US poll at all-night parties.

text.p: American expatriates stayed up through the night or rose before dawn in countries around the world to follow the outcome of the U.S. presidential election.
Whether toasting Bill Clinton's re-election or mourning Bob Dole's defeat, many of the estimated 3.5 million Americans living overseas gathered at parties to munch hamburgers, pancakes and doughnuts.
Many who had battled through bureaucratic hurdles to obtain and dispatch absentee ballots to their home states spent the night casting their votes in straw polls.
More than 1,000 Americans and Germans packed the "Amerika Haus" in Berlin for an all-night party. In Rome the U.S. Embassy hosted a party at the Excelsior Hotel that stretched into the early hours.
At the U.S. Embassy in Paris, hundreds of Americans briefly put down their fried chicken and nachos to burst out singing the American national anthem in the middle of the night.
In Madrid Americans partied till dawn amid red, white and blue balloons to the sound of a country-and-western band.

In Ireland, which has around half of its 80-million diaspora dotted throughout the United States, people stayed up to toast Clinton's success at winning a second White House term with Guinness beer and hot dogs.
At the Amerika Haus, the crowd erupted into a deafening roar at 3 a.m. when Clinton was proclaimed the winner by U.S. television networks.
"It's a good mix of Americans and Germans," said cultural attache Scott Rauland. "The Germans want to experience an American election party. German elections are much more sober."

There were also early morning suit-and-tie power breakfasts in European cities such as Bonn, Frankfurt, Madrid and Helsinki, where scrambled eggs and bacon along with uniquely weak American coffee greeted invitation-only guests.
The once-neglected expatriate vote has become coveted by both major parties since 1988, when one senatorial race in Florida was overturned by absentee ballots.
In London, about 1,500 people followed the vote count on a huge television screen in the auditorium of the embassy.
"We held on to Congress, that's what we're happy about," said Anne Collins, chairwoman of Republicans Abroad in Britain.

After Canada and Mexico, Germany has the highest number of American expatriates with just under 400,000. There are also large numbers of Americans in Britain, Italy, France and Israel. Americans have voted with absentee ballots since the mid-1970s.
But in Paris, the Americans have been casting their votes in a famous straw poll at Harry's New York Bar since 1924.
The patrons at America's most famous overseas watering hole have picked the actual winner every time except in 1976. The drinkers were right again -- 441 for Clinton and 435 for Dole.
"The atmosphere was like a convention," said Mary Beth Barent of the French capital's Association of Americans Resident Overseas.

In Rome, U.S. ambassador Reginald Bartholomew hosted a party for expatriates and Italian politicians, businessmen and celebrities with cross-cultural specialities such as pasta, mortadella, hamburgers and doughnuts.
Italo-American Mario Cuomo, the former governor of New York, addressed the crowd in a live satellite link-up from the states.
The U.S. polls shut as the sun was rising in Tokyo, where American businessmen and U.S. marines on Okinawa paused only briefly in the middle of their work day to find out the outcome.
In Warsaw, Americans chewed on burgers and doughnuts while chatting with prominent Poles including former communist military strongman Wojciech Jaruzelski, who said he liked Dole.

"I sympathise with him as a fellow former soldier -- we had similar experiences in World War Two," said the general who declared martial law in 1981. "But I think Clinton will be better, due to his (younger) age and dynamism."
